prompt: What are waxes, chemically?

choices.text: Mixtures of esters of long-chain carboxylic acids with long-chain alcohols
Triesters of glycerol with three long-chain fatty acids
choices.why: That describes fats and oils (triacylglycerols). Waxes are esters of a long-chain acid with a long-chain alcohol, not with glycerol.

choices.text: Esters of phosphoric acid with glycerol and an amino alcohol
choices.why: That describes glycerophospholipids. Waxes are carboxylic acid esters of long-chain alcohols.

choices.text: Sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids
choices.why: That describes soap. Waxes are neutral esters, not salts.

explanation: Waxes are mixtures of esters of long-chain carboxylic acids with long-chain alcohols. The acid usually has an even number of carbons from 16 to 36, and the alcohol an even number from 24 to 36.

prompt: Triacontyl hexadecanoate, a major component of beeswax, is the ester of the C30 alcohol 1-triacontanol and the C16 acid hexadecanoic acid. How many carbon atoms does one molecule of the ester contain?
explanation: Forming an ester keeps all the carbons of both parts: 30 from 1-triacontanol plus 16 from hexadecanoic acid gives 46 carbons.

prompt: Carnauba wax contains an ester of a C32 straight-chain alcohol with a C20 straight-chain carboxylic acid. Which condensed formula is that ester?

choices.text: CH3(CH2)18CO2CH2(CH2)30CH3
CH3(CH2)30CO2CH2(CH2)18CH3
choices.why: This has the parts swapped: a C32 acid and a C20 alcohol. The acid part, CH3(CH2)18CO2–, should have 20 carbons, and the alcohol part, –CH2(CH2)30CH3, should have 32.

choices.text: CH3(CH2)20CO2CH2(CH2)32CH3
choices.why: Count the carbons: CH3(CH2)20CO2– has 22 carbons and –CH2(CH2)32CH3 has 34. Both parts are two carbons too long.

choices.text: CH3(CH2)18CO2H + HOCH2(CH2)30CH3
choices.why: These are the separate acid and alcohol that make up the wax, not the ester itself.

explanation: In Exercise 27.1.1 the C20 acid supplies CH3(CH2)18CO2– (19 carbons in the chain plus the carbonyl carbon) and the C32 alcohol supplies –CH2(CH2)30CH3 (32 carbons), giving CH3(CH2)18CO2CH2(CH2)30CH3.

prompt: What are animal fats and vegetable oils, chemically?

choices.text: Triesters of glycerol with three long-chain carboxylic acids
Esters of a long-chain carboxylic acid with a long-chain alcohol
choices.why: That describes waxes. Fats and oils are esters of glycerol, a triol, with three fatty acids.

choices.text: Diesters of glycerol with two fatty acids and one phosphoric acid
choices.why: That is phosphatidic acid, the parent of the glycerophospholipids (Section 27.3).

choices.text: Long-chain carboxylic acids that are not esterified
choices.why: Free fatty acids are what hydrolysis of a fat gives. The fat itself is a triester.

explanation: Fats and oils are triglycerides, or triacylglycerols: triesters of glycerol with three long-chain carboxylic acids called fatty acids. Butter and lard are solids and corn oil is a liquid, but their structures are closely related.

prompt: About how many times as much energy do fats provide as an equal weight of stored, hydrated glycogen?
explanation: Animals use fats for long-term energy storage because fats are far less highly oxidized than carbohydrates and provide about six times as much energy as an equal weight of stored, hydrated glycogen.

prompt: Hydrolysis of one triacylglycerol molecule with aqueous NaOH gives one glycerol. How many fatty acids does it give?
explanation: A triacylglycerol is a triester of glycerol, so hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH breaks all three ester bonds and gives glycerol and three fatty acids. The three need not be the same.

prompt: Which description fits the fatty acids obtained from fats and oils?

choices.text: Generally unbranched, with an even number of carbons between 12 and 20
Generally branched, with an odd number of carbons between 13 and 21
choices.why: The section says fatty acids are generally unbranched and contain an even number of carbon atoms.

choices.text: Unbranched, with an even number of carbons between 16 and 36
choices.why: That range belongs to the carboxylic acids in waxes. Fatty acids from fats and oils have 12 to 20 carbons.

choices.text: Unbranched, with double bonds that mostly have E, or trans, geometry
choices.why: Double bonds in natural fatty acids mostly have Z, or cis, geometry.

explanation: Fatty acids from fats and oils are generally unbranched and contain an even number of carbon atoms between 12 and 20. Any double bonds are mostly, though not entirely, Z (cis).

prompt: Arachidonic acid is (all Z)-CH3(CH2)4(CH=CHCH2)4CH2CH2CO2H. How many carbon–carbon double bonds does it contain?
explanation: The repeating unit (CH=CHCH2) appears 4 times, and each contains one C=C bond, so arachidonic acid has 4 double bonds. With more than one double bond, it is a polyunsaturated fatty acid.

prompt: Palmitoleic acid is (Z)-CH3(CH2)5CH=CH(CH2)7CO2H. How many carbon atoms does it contain?
explanation: Count the pieces: CH3 (1) + (CH2)5 (5) + CH=CH (2) + (CH2)7 (7) + CO2H (1) = 16. Table 27.1.1 lists palmitoleic acid as a C16 unsaturated fatty acid.

prompt: Linoleic acid, (Z,Z)-CH3(CH2)4(CH=CHCH2)2(CH2)6CO2H, is classified as which kind of fatty acid?

choices.text: Polyunsaturated
Monounsaturated
choices.why: A monounsaturated fatty acid such as oleic acid has only one double bond. Linoleic acid has two.

choices.text: Saturated
choices.why: Saturated fatty acids such as stearic acid have no C=C bonds. Linoleic acid has two.

choices.text: A trans fatty acid
choices.why: Its double bonds are both Z (cis), as the (Z,Z) label shows.

explanation: Oleic acid is monounsaturated because it has only one double bond, whereas linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic acids are polyunsaturated because they have more than one double bond.

prompt: What does the name omega-3 fatty acid mean?

choices.text: There is a double bond three carbons in from the noncarboxyl end of the chain
There is a double bond three carbons in from the carboxyl end of the chain
choices.why: The count starts from the other end, the noncarboxyl (methyl) end of the chain.

choices.text: The fatty acid contains exactly three double bonds
choices.why: The name refers to the position of a double bond, not the number of double bonds.

choices.text: The fatty acid contains three fewer carbons than stearic acid
choices.why: The name says nothing about chain length; it gives a double-bond position counted from the noncarboxyl end.

explanation: The name omega-3 means that there is a double bond three carbons in from the noncarboxyl end of the chain. Linolenic acid is an example; omega-3 fatty acids have been found to lower blood triglyceride levels and reduce the risk of heart attack.

prompt: Using Table 27.1.1's structures, which fatty acid is an omega-3 fatty acid?

choices.text: Linolenic acid, (all Z)-CH3CH2(CH=CHCH2)3(CH2)6CO2H
Oleic acid, (Z)-CH3(CH2)7CH=CH(CH2)7CO2H
choices.why: Counting from the CH3 end, oleic acid's double bond starts at the ninth carbon, not the third.

choices.text: Arachidonic acid, (all Z)-CH3(CH2)4(CH=CHCH2)4CH2CH2CO2H
choices.why: Counting from the CH3 end, the first double bond starts at the sixth carbon (CH3 plus four CH2 groups come first).

choices.text: Stearic acid, CH3(CH2)16CO2H
choices.why: Stearic acid is saturated and has no double bonds at all.

explanation: In linolenic acid, CH3 is the first carbon from the noncarboxyl end, CH2 the second, and the third begins the first CH=CH. The section names linolenic acid as an example of an omega-3 fatty acid.

prompt: Stearic acid and oleic acid both have 18 carbons. Stearic acid melts at 68.8 °C and oleic acid, with one cis double bond, melts at 13.4 °C. How many degrees lower is the melting point of oleic acid?
explanation: 68.8 °C − 13.4 °C = 55.4 °C. Table 27.1.1 shows that unsaturated fatty acids generally have lower melting points than their saturated counterparts, because the cis C=C bond puts a kink in the chain that makes packing in a crystal harder.

prompt: Why do vegetable oils generally have lower melting points than animal fats?

choices.text: Their higher share of unsaturated fatty acids puts kinks in the chains, so the molecules pack into a crystal less easily
Their fatty acids are shorter, mostly with fewer than 12 carbons
choices.why: The fatty acids in both fats and oils mostly have 12 to 20 carbons; Table 27.1.2 lists mainly C16 and C18 acids in oils. The difference is unsaturation.

choices.text: Their fatty acids contain more trans double bonds, which make the chains straighter
choices.why: Natural fatty acids have mostly cis double bonds, and it is those cis C=C bonds that bend the chains.

choices.text: They contain glycerol diesters instead of triesters
choices.why: Both fats and oils are triacylglycerols, triesters of glycerol.

explanation: Vegetable oils have a higher proportion of unsaturated to saturated fatty acids than animal fats (Table 27.1.2). Saturated chains have a uniform shape that packs well in a crystal lattice; C=C bonds introduce bends and kinks that make crystal formation harder. The more double bonds, the lower the melting point.

prompt: According to Table 27.1.2, coconut oil contains 50% lauric, 18% myristic, 8% palmitic, and 2% stearic acid. What total percentage of its fatty acids are these saturated ones?
explanation: 50% + 18% + 8% + 2% = 78%. Coconut oil is unusual among the vegetable oils in Table 27.1.2: most of its fatty acids are saturated, while corn, olive, and peanut oils are mostly oleic and linoleic acids.

prompt: Glyceryl tripalmitate is the triester of glycerol (3 carbons) with three molecules of palmitic acid (C16). How many carbon atoms does one molecule contain?
explanation: Esterification keeps every carbon: 3 from glycerol plus 3 × 16 = 48 from the palmitoyl groups gives 51 carbons.

prompt: Which would you expect to have the higher melting point, glyceryl tripalmitate or glyceryl trioleate?

choices.text: Glyceryl tripalmitate, because its saturated chains pack together efficiently
Glyceryl trioleate, because its chains are two carbons longer
choices.why: Chain length isn't the deciding factor here. Oleic acid's cis double bond kinks the chain and lowers the melting point.

choices.text: Glyceryl trioleate, because its double bonds make the molecules more rigid
choices.why: The cis double bonds introduce bends and kinks that make crystal formation harder, lowering the melting point.

choices.text: They melt at the same temperature, because both are triacylglycerols
choices.why: Unsaturation changes the melting point; the saturated triacylglycerol melts higher.

explanation: As Exercise 27.1.2 answers, glyceryl tripalmitate is higher melting. Palmitic acid is saturated, while oleic acid has a cis double bond; unsaturated triacylglycerols, like unsaturated fatty acids, have lower melting points.

prompt: How are the C=C bonds in vegetable oils reduced to make solid or semisolid fats?

choices.text: By catalytic hydrogenation at high temperature using a nickel catalyst
By hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH
choices.why: Hydrolysis with NaOH breaks the ester bonds to give glycerol and fatty acids; it doesn't reduce C=C bonds.

choices.text: By isomerizing the cis double bonds to trans with a nickel catalyst
choices.why: Some cis–trans isomerization does happen as a side reaction, but the purpose is to reduce the C=C bonds by adding hydrogen.

choices.text: By cooling the oil until it crystallizes
choices.why: Cooling doesn't change the structure. Removing the C=C bonds requires a chemical reduction, catalytic hydrogenation.

explanation: The C=C bonds in vegetable oils can be reduced by catalytic hydrogenation, typically at high temperature with a nickel catalyst, to give saturated solid or semisolid fats. Before 2015, margarine and shortening were made this way from soybean, peanut, or cottonseed oil.

prompt: What unwanted side reaction accompanies the industrial hydrogenation of vegetable oils?

choices.text: Cis–trans isomerization of the remaining double bonds, giving about 10% to 15% trans fatty acids
Hydrolysis of the ester bonds, giving free glycerol
choices.why: The section doesn't describe hydrolysis during hydrogenation. The problem is cis–trans isomerization of the double bonds that remain.

choices.text: Migration of the double bonds into conjugation with the ester carbonyl
choices.why: The section describes isomerization of cis double bonds to trans, not migration of double bonds.

choices.text: Trans–cis isomerization, giving more cis double bonds than were present in the oil
choices.why: The direction is the reverse: natural cis double bonds are partly converted to trans.

explanation: Hydrogenation is accompanied by some cis–trans isomerization of the remaining double bonds, producing fats with about 10% to 15% trans unsaturated fatty acids. The conversion of linoleic acid into elaidic acid, whose double bond is trans, is an example. Dietary trans fatty acids raise blood cholesterol levels.

prompt: Which two fatty acids does the section describe as essential in the human diet?

choices.text: Linoleic and linolenic acids
Palmitic and stearic acids
choices.why: These are the most abundant saturated fatty acids, not the essential ones.

choices.text: Oleic and elaidic acids
choices.why: Oleic acid is monounsaturated and elaidic acid is a trans fatty acid formed during hydrogenation; neither is named as essential.

choices.text: Lauric and myristic acids
choices.why: These are saturated fatty acids found, for example, in coconut oil; they are not named as essential.

explanation: Linoleic and linolenic acids occur in cream and are essential in the human diet. Infants grow poorly and develop skin lesions if fed nonfat milk for prolonged periods.
